checks.caption: the product's shape changed: a part reshaped, moved or merged
checks.check: The clown's object, unchanged. The same parts, in the same number, with the same silhouette, the same parting lines and the same pose as the clown. Only the surfaces change.
checks.fails_when: A part reshaped, resized, moved, merged with another or split in two; a silhouette that no longer lies on the clown's; a parting line gone, moved or added

checks.caption: a clown colour is still on the product
checks.check: No clown colour left. Every zone the key maps has lost its clown colour and taken its row's colour, all the way to its edges and into its shadows.
checks.fails_when: Any zone, or part of one, still in the clown's flat colour or a near shade of it: a whole part, a patch in shadow, a rim along a parting line, a tint the new colour did not cover

checks.caption: a colour or finish is on the wrong part
checks.check: Each zone is its component. The colour, material and finish of each row sit on the zone the key names for that component, and nowhere else.
checks.fails_when: Two components' specs swapped; a spec bleeding across a parting line onto the next part; a zone given a colour, material or finish its row does not hold

checks.caption: something added or missing: text, a logo, a part
checks.check: Nothing added, nothing removed. The render holds what the clown holds and nothing else.
checks.fails_when: Text, a logo, a marking or a label the clown does not carry and the row does not name; a hand, a prop, packaging, a second object; or a part, a marking or a component the key places on this clown gone missing

checks.caption: the colour does not read as its code
checks.check: Reads as the code. Each zone's colour reads as its row's code: as the confirmed hex THE ROW carries for it where there is one, else as the colour name the sheet gives beside the code.
checks.fails_when: A hue, lightness or saturation that someone holding the Pantone chip would call another colour; or a code with neither a hex nor a name judged from memory instead of reported as not judged

checks.caption: a part is not one colour, or its pattern is wrong
checks.check: One colour per zone, unless the row names a pattern. Each zone is one even colour, shaded only by the light, unless its row names a pattern or an effect (marble, speckle, two-tone). A named pattern is drawn in the row's own codes, in the proportion the row gives where it gives one.
checks.fails_when: A second colour, a gradient, a blotch or a stripe on a zone whose row names one colour; or a named pattern drawn in colours the row does not hold, reading as something else, or not drawn at all

checks.caption: parts with the same code do not match
checks.check: Shared codes match. Components the row gives the same code read as the same colour, allowing for their different materials and finishes.
checks.fails_when: Two parts with one code that read as two colours under the same light

checks.caption: the translucency is wrong: see-through where it should be opaque, or the reverse
checks.check: Translucency as specified. A part the row calls milky, frosted or see-through lets light through its thin edges, as much as the row's percentage says; a part the row does not call translucent is opaque.
checks.fails_when: A translucent part drawn opaque or clear as glass; an opaque part drawn see-through; the inside of the product showing through a part that should hide it

checks.caption: wrong finish: gloss for matte, matte for gloss
checks.check: Finish family. Each part reads as its row's finish, as the Grading rules describe it: matte, a VDI grain, satin, NCVM, gloss, mirror, grinded.
checks.fails_when: Gloss for matte, matte for gloss, a mirror where the row says satin, a smooth surface where the row gives a VDI grain, or one finish laid over parts the row gives different finishes

checks.caption: the material does not read as its material
checks.check: Material behaviour. Each part behaves as its material: silicone soft, with a rubbery sheen; ABS, PC and POM moulded plastic; aluminium anodised metal; textile with a visible weave or knit; foam soft and open; a TPE cord supple and matte.
checks.fails_when: A silicone part that reads as hard plastic or glass; a plastic part that reads as bare metal with no NCVM or anodising in its row; a metal part that reads as painted plastic; a textile that reads as a moulded surface

checks.caption: the texture is coarser or finer than specified
checks.check: Texture at the specified grade. A VDI or grain value in the row shows as that grade, the same on every part that shares the value.
checks.fails_when: A texture visibly coarser or finer than its grade, a texture on a part whose row gives none, or two parts with one grade drawn at two

checks.caption: a coating or effect is missing, wrong or in the wrong place
checks.check: Coatings and effects. NCVM, holographic, UV gloss, marble and every other effect the row names appear where it names them, embedded in the material, and nowhere else.
checks.fails_when: An effect missing, painted on top like a sticker, spread onto a part whose row does not give it, or an effect no row names

checks.caption: the artwork is missing, wrong or where it should not be
checks.check: Artwork and logos where the row says. Where the key maps a zone to artwork, it carries the row's artwork colour and technique; where a component's artwork cell is a `/`, the part carries none.
checks.fails_when: Artwork missing where the row and the key place it, in the wrong colour or technique (printed where the row says embossed), or present on a part whose artwork cell is a `/`

checks.caption: relit
checks.check: Lighting unchanged. The light falls as it does on the clown: the same direction, the same softness, highlights and shadows in the same places.
checks.fails_when: The render relit: a key light moved, a rim light or a warm or cool cast added, shadows deepened, softened or removed, a studio mood the clown does not have

checks.caption: the background changed
checks.check: Background unchanged. The ground behind and under the product is the clown's, in tone and colour.
checks.fails_when: A new colour, gradient, texture, floor, reflection or shadow behind or under the product

checks.caption: the camera moved or the crop changed
checks.check: Camera and framing unchanged. The same angle, lens, crop, position and size in the frame as the clown.
checks.fails_when: The product moved, rotated, zoomed, recropped or seen from another angle; a perspective that no longer matches the clown

checks.caption: soft or ragged edges where two parts meet
checks.check: Edges at parting lines. Where two components meet, the change of colour and finish runs along the parting line, crisp at the scale of the image.
checks.fails_when: A soft halo, a ragged or stepped edge, a gap, or a colour that stops short of the line or runs past it

checks.caption: an artefact in the image
checks.check: The image is otherwise sound. No artefact a viewer would notice: banding, noise, smears, doubled edges, compression blocks.
checks.fails_when: Any artefact a viewer would notice before they notice the part

checks.caption: cropped, too small or the wrong shape
checks.check: Whole and full size. The product is whole in the frame, and the image is at the size the payload asked for and at the clown's aspect.
checks.fails_when: A part cut by the frame edge, an image smaller than the size asked for, or an aspect other than the clown's

rubric.grading_rules:
The grader reads this section into its prompt verbatim.

- **Two images, named.** Image 1 is the candidate render. Image 2 is the clown model it was drawn
  from: the same object with each component painted one flat colour, shaded, on its own ground.
  Judge the candidate against the clown, side by side, never against what you think the product
  looks like.
- **THE ROW is the spec.** The sheet row for this SKU is quoted under THE ROW: each component with
  its material, finish, colour name and code, as the sheet wrote them. A colour, material, finish or
  effect the row does not hold is not in the spec, however plausible it looks.
- **THE KEY is the map.** Quoted under THE KEY: each clown colour as a hex, the component or
  components it marks, and the components that are not on this clown. A zone that serves two
  components names both. A component the key says is not on this clown is absent by design, never
  missing.
- **The measurements are evidence, not verdict.** MEASUREMENTS states per zone, in words, how much of
  it is still within reach of the clown's colour and, where the code has a confirmed hex, how far
  the zone's colour sits from it. They tell you where to look; they do not decide. A note that
  ignores a large leftover share is an incomplete note.
- **What each finish word looks like.** Judge a finish by how the part takes the light:
  - *matte*: diffuse, no specular hotspot, the light falls off softly across the form.
  - *VDI 18 to VDI 27*: a spark-eroded grain that scatters the light evenly; near smooth-matte at
    VDI 18, a fine visible grain at VDI 24, coarser at VDI 27; never glossy.
  - *satin*: a soft sheen with broad, blurred highlights. *NCVM*: a metallic sheen on a plastic
    part, highlights that follow the form like metal, no brushed grain unless the row says so.
  - *gloss*, *high gloss*, *mirror*: sharp specular highlights and clear reflections of the light.
  - *grinded*, *grinding*: an abraded, frosted surface, even, with the highlights broken up.
  - *milky*, *frosted*, *see-through*, with or without a percentage: translucent, light passing
    through the thin edges and a soft glow in the body, more the higher the percentage; never clear
    like glass, never opaque.
  - *opaque*: no light through the part at any edge.
  - *holographic*, *iridescent*, *pearlescent*: the colour shifts with the angle, inside the
    material, not a sticker on top.
  - *anodised*: coloured metal with a fine metallic sheen and an even tone, brushed or polished as
    the row says.
  - *pad print*, *silk screen*: flat ink on the surface, crisp edges, no relief. *embossed*,
    *debossed*: relief in the material itself, in the part's own colour unless the row names one.
- **Absence and leftover are the usual misses.** Graders flag what is wrong and skip what is still
  there. The likeliest misses on this work: a zone, or a rim of one along a parting line, still in
  the clown's colour (the Experience 2 carry case shells came back red); a part given no finish; a
  part that disappeared. Look for the clown's colours first.
- **Judge what the view shows.** A component the key says is not on this clown, or one hidden by the
  angle, passes its check; a component shown wrongly fails it.
- **Fail when unsure**, and say in the note what you could not see.

grading_prompt.anatomy:
One continuous, wide, curved head strap with the eye cups built into its middle, plus a separate removable eye pad that presses into the cups from the inside.
Strap (exterior and interior): knit textile, 85 % polyamide / 15 % elastane, 130 GSM. Matte. At close range a fine rib runs *along* the band (horizontal when worn). No sheen, no weave pattern, no satin, no neoprene grain. Flat-lay reference: Loop_Eclipse-Black-Flatlay Back-Open-Washing Label Update (Frontify, Eclipse/Renders/Product Renders) shows the whole band opened out.
Eye cups: two low oblong pockets formed in the band itself, joined over a nose notch. Each is a wide oval in outline, wider than it is tall and shallow: it stands off the eye by roughly a fifth of its width, which is the room the eyes and eyelashes need (Frontify graphic Eyelash_Clearance). The top edge of each pocket is the top edge of the band, one continuous line with no step. The two pockets meet over the nose in a shallow saddle: seen from the front, three-quarter or above, the outer face of the cup section reads as one smooth, low, continuous form whose top edge runs as a single unbroken arc (Loop_Eclipse-Plum-05 Angle 1), and what marks the two pockets is the nose notch cut into the lower edge, with the surface rising to either side of it. The transition from band to pocket is a soft rounded edge in the knit, not a stitched seam and not a raised ring (Loop_Eclipse-Black-05 Angle 1). They are not hemispheres, not padded cups fixed onto a flat band, and not a moulded foam shell. Both pockets are the same size.
Eye pad (removable): a symmetrical foam piece shaped like the two cups with the nose notch; peels off the strap for washing. Reference: second row of the flat-lay render.
Ear scoop: between the eye cups and the back, the lower edge of the band rises in a deep concave arc. The band passes above the ear; the ear sits in the scoop and stays visible below the strap. Reference: Loop_Eclipse-Teal-Side_2 and the Eyelash_Clearance graphic.
Closure end (back of the head): hook-and-loop. One strap end carries, from the tip inward, the round O-logo patch (a ring with the care icons printed inside it) and then a black matte silicone patch with a row of curved ridges, the tactile guides (three to five concentric arcs). The other end carries the plain hook-and-loop field. When the mask is closed the tip with the O-logo is usually hidden by the overlap, so a view can show the ridges and not the O-logo and be correct. Anti-slip silicone sits on the inside of the band. Reference: both ends in the flat-lay render; the ridged patch in Loop_Eclipse-Teal-Side_2 and Loop_Eclipse-Plum-05 Angle 1.
Wordmark: "loop", lowercase, small, white, printed flat on the outer flank of the eye-cup section toward the temple, near the top edge, reading along the band. One per side. Seen from the front it sits on the temple-side edge of the cup; on a side sleeper it can stand vertical in the frame because the head is on its side, and that is correct. Product reference: Loop_Eclipse-Teal-Side_2; in wear: LOOP_Eclipse_1029-final (frontal) and loop-eclipse-lifestyle-05 (side). Never embossed, never metal, never a second wordmark, never "Loop Eclipse" written on the product.
Interior face: dark (black or near-black) where visible, on every colourway (Loop_Eclipse-Plum-05 Angle 1).
Nothing else on the product. No buckle, no slider, no second strap, no nose bridge piece, no visible foam, no elastic cord, no zip, no tag on the outside.

grading_prompt.rules:
The grader reads this section into its prompt verbatim.

- **The stranger's read comes first.** Before the checks, a separate call that saw only the candidate, with no product name, no references and no product sheet, named the object on the face in one phrase and described its eye section in one sentence. Both are quoted under THIS CANDIDATE, and A6 is graded as that reader saw it, not as you know the product to be. A word from the Object-class words list in that phrase forces A6 in code, whatever you answer.
- **Judge what the view shows.** A part hidden by the angle passes its check; a part shown wrongly fails it. A profile hides the far cup; a frontal hides the closure; a flat-lay hides the wear; the strap overlap hides the tip of the strap end.
- **Know the asset class.** *Product*: the bare mask or render. *Wear*: a person wearing it. *Composite*: a finished channel deliverable with headline, badges, callouts, other Loop products. Loop's own products and typography are normal in a composite and never count as invented.
- **The colourway claim.** A claim from library metadata is untrusted. A colourway token in the title or a reviewer's statement is trusted. With no trusted claim, identify the colourway from the image and say so.
- **Absence is the usual miss.** Graders over-penalise excess and under-penalise absence. The likeliest misses on this product are flat fabric where the two eye pockets should be (B2), a missing ear scoop (B5), a missing wordmark (A2), a knit with no rib (C1). Look for what is not there.
- **The numbers are evidence.** The measurement layer's textile lightness, chroma and hue distance to the colourway band are attached to every grade. They do not decide; they tell you where to look, and a note that ignores a large distance is an incomplete note.
- **Fail when unsure**, and say in the note what you could not see.

text.candidate: Image 1 is the CANDIDATE under review. Grade image 1, and only image 1.
text.claim_detected: There is no trusted colourway claim. Read from the image, the textile looks like {detected} (confidence {confidence}). Judge D1 against that colourway, and fail E3 if the textile is ambiguous between two colourways.
text.claim_none: There is no trusted colourway claim and the colourway could not be read from the image. Identify it yourself; if it is ambiguous, E3 fails.
text.claim_trusted: Trusted colourway claim: {claim} (from the {source}). Judge D1 against that colourway, and fail E3 if the image disagrees with it.
text.claim_untrusted: The library's metadata says {claim}, and library metadata is NOT a trusted claim. Do not treat it as one.
text.crop: Image 1b is the CANDIDATE's mask region enlarged, for texture and cup shape; it is the same picture as image 1.
text.intro: You are grading one candidate image of the Loop Eclipse sleep mask for the Loop studio team, with the real product on the desk beside you. Read the image as someone who has never seen the brief.
text.json_intro: Return ONLY JSON, no fences, every check id present:
text.missing: Some pinned references are missing locally and are not attached: {items}. Grade without them and be correspondingly careful.
text.product_heading: THE PRODUCT, from the product sheet:
text.references_are_real: References are the real product. They are never under review, and a difference between the candidate and a reference is a fault in the CANDIDATE.
text.restate: Before the checks, in your own words: name the object in this image in one short noun phrase (reads_as) and describe the part of it that sits over the eyes in one sentence (cup_section). Answer those two first, then grade. A description you have committed to is what the checks are graded against.
text.role_default: a reference photograph of the real product.

roles.cross_section: a cross-section LINE DRAWING of how far the eye cup stands off the eye. Use it for cup depth (B2) and for nothing else: it is a diagram, so it says nothing about texture, colour, print or light.
roles.flat_lay: the product opened flat — every part of the real product at once. Use it for anatomy, part inventory and closure ends.
roles.side: the side render of the real product. Every profile or three-quarter candidate must agree with this geometry: ear scoop, wordmark placement, the ridged silicone patch, cup depth. The O-logo at the tip of the strap end is hidden by the overlap here, and that is correct.
roles.wear_face: a live photograph of the real product worn and lit so the outer face of the eye section can be read. Compare the candidate's eye section with it.
roles.wear_frontal: a live photograph of the real product being worn. Use it for how the band sits, how the cup compresses and where the wordmark falls.

text.stranger_check: Grade {check} as that reader saw it.
text.stranger_cup_section: They described its eye section as: "{cup_section}".
text.stranger_no_check: Grade the check that asks how the object reads to a stranger as that reader saw it.
text.stranger_reads_as: A reader who saw only this image, with no references and no brief, called the object: "{reads_as}".
text.strict: Grade every check strictly true (passes) or false (fails). When you are unsure, the check FAILS. Judge only what this image shows; do not credit the candidate for anything you cannot see.

Grade the object as that reader saw it.

checks.caption: the band is too thin or too rigid
checks.check: Band width. The strap is wide and flat, about twice as tall at the eye cups as at the temple, and still a broad band at the back.
checks.fails_when: Reads as a thin headband or elastic, or as a rigid goggle frame

checks.caption: the eye pockets are wrong: one dome, flat, or ball-shaped cups
checks.check: Two low pockets, not one dome and not two balls. Two shallow oblong pockets, each a wide oval in outline, much wider than it is tall and much wider than it is deep, formed in the band itself: the band pushed forward, not a cup fixed onto it. The top edge of each pocket runs on as the top edge of the band, with no step and no seam. The two pockets meet over the nose in a shallow saddle, and the outer face of the cup section is one smooth, low, continuous form: from the front, three-quarter or above, the top edge can run as a single unbroken arc and the surface between the pockets settles only slightly, and that is the product. What marks two pockets rather than one is the nose notch cut into the lower edge over the bridge of the nose, with the surface rising to either side of it. In profile the pocket stands off the face by a fraction of its width and its lower edge dips to the nose bridge rather than running straight across. In wear the pocket compresses, and on a side sleeper with the cup pressed into a pillow it can read almost flat; that too is the product. Flat fails only when there is no pocket at all: the fabric follows the eyelids and the brow with no raised outline anywhere.
checks.fails_when: A cup section with no nose notch in its lower edge and no rise to either side of the nose, one bulge from temple to temple; fabric that follows the eyelids with no pocket outline anywhere; or a cup drawn as a hemisphere or ball: round in outline, about as tall as it is wide, standing proud of a flat band like a padded cup stitched on, or so deep it reads as goggles

checks.caption: wrong size on the head, or the strap stops at the ear
checks.check: Scale on the head, and the strap goes round it. From just above the eyebrows to the top of the cheekbones, reaching past the temples. The strap continues behind the ear and round the back of the head, and the closure with its ridged silicone patch sits there, out of sight in most wear views. If the ridged patch is visible on, above or just in front of the ear, the strap has stopped at the ear and this check fails, whatever else is right.

rubric.grading_rules:
The grader reads this section into its prompt verbatim.

- **The stranger's read comes first.** Before the checks, a separate call that saw only the candidate, with no product name, no references and no product sheet, named the object on the face in one phrase and described its eye section in one sentence. Both are quoted under THIS CANDIDATE, and A6 is graded as that reader saw it, not as you know the product to be. A word from the Object-class words list in that phrase forces A6 in code, whatever you answer.
- **Judge what the view shows.** A part hidden by the angle passes its check; a part shown wrongly fails it. A profile hides the far cup; a frontal hides the closure; a flat-lay hides the wear; the strap overlap hides the tip of the strap end.
- **Know the asset class.** *Product*: the bare mask or render. *Wear*: a person wearing it. *Composite*: a finished channel deliverable with headline, badges, callouts, other Loop products. Loop's own products and typography are normal in a composite and never count as invented.
- **The colourway claim.** A claim from library metadata is untrusted. A colourway token in the title or a reviewer's statement is trusted. With no trusted claim, identify the colourway from the image and say so.
- **Absence is the usual miss.** Graders over-penalise excess and under-penalise absence. The likeliest misses on this product are flat fabric where the two eye pockets should be (B2), a missing ear scoop (B5), a missing wordmark (A2), a knit with no rib (C1). Look for what is not there.
- **The numbers are evidence.** The measurement layer's textile lightness, chroma and hue distance to the colourway band are attached to every grade. They do not decide; they tell you where to look, and a note that ignores a large distance is an incomplete note.
- **Fail when unsure**, and say in the note what you could not see.

rubric.grading_rules:
- **Judge what the scene shows.** A panel hidden by the view passes its check; a panel shown wrongly
  fails it. The closed box shows one large face and two thin walls; the open box shows the inside of
  the lid, the tray, the front flap with its round die-cut, and its outer walls.
- **The white render and the dieline are the truth.** When the candidate's own white render, composite
  and dieline are attached, judge geometry against the render and the print against the dieline. When
  they are not, say so in the note and judge against the pinned scene of the same look.
- **The numbers are evidence, not the verdict.** Where the scripts report a silhouette overlap, an
  artwork match or a per-panel colour distance, read the words in the measurement block and look for
  what in the picture explains them. A number over its line with nothing in the picture to explain it
  fails the check; a number under its line does not pass a check the eye can see failing.
- **Absence is the usual miss.** Look for the panel that is blank, the die-cut that is filled, the
  gradient that has become a flat colour, the inside print that is missing.
- **Fail when unsure**, and say in the note what you could not see.

prompting.skill_body:
# Prompting image and video models, the Loop way

Loop makes a growing share of its product imagery with image models, and the graded rounds on the
Eclipse sleep mask, the retail packaging and the CMF renders taught what holds a product true and
what does not. This skill carries those lessons. It is also the instruction Vesper's prompt tools
run on, so it is written to be read on its own.

One idea runs through all of it: **use the model for judgement, use code for data.** The product
comes from its real render, the words about it are filled in by code, and a person decides.

## First: is a Loop product in the picture?

Ask this before writing a word. The answer changes everything below it.

**Yes: a Loop product is in the picture** (the Eclipse sleep mask, a Loop earplug or case, the
retail box, a CMF colourway render of a clown model):

- **Its real render is image 1**, in the right colourway and view. The words never describe the
  product from memory.
- **The prompt is the product's skeleton, with only its slots filled**: the scene, the light, the
  format, the colourway. The product sentences are never rewritten, shortened or "improved", by you
  or by any prompt tool. Asked to enhance a product prompt, return it unchanged and say why: a model
  rewrite invents, and in Vesper's CMF history it turned Pantone 2160C into "a vivid lime green" in
  one attempt and "a muted purple-grey" in the next.
- **Never iterate from a draw.** The next draw starts again from the render, with one thing changed
  in the words.
- **The skeletons**: Eclipse's in its skill (skeleton v3); packaging's in its skill (v2, used only
  after the mockup is built in code); CMF's is Damien's template, filled from the sheet row and the
  clown's key, with the clown the only image.
- **A Loop product with no skeleton yet**: its render is still image 1, the product is named and
  never described, and only the scene is written. Say plainly that no rubric grades it yet.
- **With Vesper connected**, `generate_product_image` does this in code: it picks the pinned
  references in order, fills the skeleton, makes one call per image and records every draw. For a
  CMF row, `cmf_prompt` and `cmf_render`; for packaging, `packaging_mockup` and then
  `packaging_finish`. `enhance_prompt` returns a product prompt unchanged.

**No: nothing of Loop's is in the picture** (a mood, a world, a texture, a person with no product):
write it with full craft (below). Rewriting, enhancing and editing from a previous draw are all
allowed here.

## Job 1: you just want an image

1. **Name it**: the product, the colourway and the view. For packaging, the look, the box and the
   colourway; for CMF, the sheet's tab, column and clown.
2. **The render is image 1.** At most two more references, and each is asked only for what it
   shows: "image 2 for how it is worn". A photograph with a person in it hands that person over, so
   when the prompt asks for someone the photograph's person could be, use a render in that slot.
3. **Fill the slots**, one sentence each. Say what should be there. One prohibition per idea at
   most. Name a colour at both ends: what it is, and what it must not drift into.
4. **The model comes from the router** below. One model per round.
5. **Two draws.**
6. **One read**, labelled as one read (`chat x1`), and shown with the product rubric's
   plain-language captions, never bare check ids.
7. **Keep, redo, or change one thing.** A defect that survives two well-aimed draws means switching
   the model or fixing it in code. A third rewrite of the prompt is the wrong move.
8. **One record line**: the date, the product, the model, the skeleton version, the draws, which was
   kept, and how it was read.

The person decides. A read is a floor, never an approval.

## Job 2: taking work to the studio, or comparing two ways of working

- **Three reads per draw**, the majority per check. With Vesper, `grade_image` does it and labels it
  `vesper x3`.
- **A second judge beside the first, never pooled.** Report what each keeps and what both keep.
- **Judge the set**: the draws side by side, the colour measured in code against the product's band.
  A drift invisible in one frame is obvious across twelve.
- **The review page**, never loose files. The person who decides verdicts there.
- **Verdicts in their words**, dated, never paraphrased.
- **One change per comparison, one model per arm.** One grade per draw at these batch sizes is a
  coin: a re-grade of untouched pixels once moved an arm by twenty-two points.
- **The record**, in the same session.

## Rules that hold everywhere

Each rule is a lesson in `references/craft.md`, with the round that taught it.

1. **The render is image 1.** A description from memory drifts; the render does not.
2. **Never a draw as the next reference.** What drifts in one draw is copied into the next, and
   nobody approved the second hop.
3. **Three references at most, each with one job.** Every extra image is one more thing to lend.
4. **A person in a reference hands themselves over**: face, hair, clothes, bedding. Cropping did not
   stop it; only removing the photograph did.
5. **A second image lends everything in it**, not only what it was asked for: its light, its print,
   its colour.
6. **The scene sets the view**, not a flag. Asked for profile on eighteen draws, a model drew
   three-quarter on seventeen. Read the view off the draw.
7. **One word can move every draw, and the grader with it.** "A wide shallow oval" drew a traced
   oval on each eye, and a grader reading the same word passed it.
8. **Say what is there.** A sentence about an object gets the object; a list of forbidden things is
   a menu.
9. **Name a colour at both ends and measure it in code.** Naming both ends halved Eclipse Teal's
   blue drift; the eye and the grader never saw it one frame at a time.
10. **No model rewrites a product prompt.** A rewrite invents colour words and guesses zones.
11. **Hold the light fixed across a set.** Light that changes by attempt changes the colour.
12. **What code can place, code places**: the packaging mockup, small type, a pad. Round 1 of
    packaging kept no model draw; the mockup in code, with only the grain from a draw, passed.
13. **A pinned reference is sent byte for byte.** A model that refuses its size is a finding, not a
    reason to resize.
14. **Pad, never crop**, when a model does not draw the product's frame.
15. **Two draws, then switch.** Change one thing at a time, and log every draw, kept or not.
16. **Grade three times; judges are never pooled; the person decides.**

## Which model

Dated 2026-09-23. The full router, the per-model notes and the reference limits are in
`references/models.md`.

| Job | First | Then |
|---|---|---|
| Product stills and wear shots | GPT Image 2 (`gpt-image-2`): kept by both judges on 10 of 12 in round 11 | Nano Banana Pro (`gemini-3-pro-image`): 5 of 12 |
| Drafts and first looks | Nano Banana 2 (`gemini-3.1-flash-image`) | |
| Packaging finish, after the mockup | Nano Banana Pro, for the surface only | |
| CMF recolour of a clown | Nano Banana Pro; the benchmark is pending | Nano Banana 2 for drafts |
| Look development, no product | Midjourney, by hand | |
| Video | no Loop round yet | |

Never send `input_fidelity` to GPT Image 2: the API rejects it. Nano Banana Pro garbles small type,
so type is placed in code.

## When no Loop product is in the picture

**Two kinds of model.** Semantic models (Nano Banana, GPT Image 2) understand intent: write to them
like a collaborator, in sentences. Descriptive models (Midjourney, most diffusion models) respond
to the density and precision of description.

**Describe the scene; do not list keywords.** A paragraph beats a pile of words. Cover, in natural
order: the subject (physical detail, clothing, pose), the environment (place, props, time of day),
the camera (lens, angle, framing, depth of field), the light (source, direction, temperature,
quality) and the look.

    Photorealistic photograph of a middle-aged woman with greying brown hair tied back loosely,
    wearing a faded olive apron over a cream linen shirt. She stands at a wooden kitchen counter,
    hands resting on a cutting board with fresh herbs. Morning light from a window camera-left
    makes soft shadows. 50mm lens at eye level, shallow depth of field. Natural skin texture,
    unprocessed.

**Name both ends** of what matters: a colour, a light, a mood, as what it is and what it must not
become.

**Say what you want, not what you do not.** Not "no dramatic lighting" but "flat even light, matte
surfaces". Describe actions, not emotions: not "looks sad" but "the corners of her mouth turn
slightly down".

**For a naturalistic look**, avoid cinematic, dramatic, epic, stunning, masterpiece; use
documentary, naturalistic, candid, ungraded.

**Label each reference's role** when there are several: a STYLE reference (match the look, never
recreate its scene), a CHARACTER reference (match this person), an OBJECT reference (reproduce this
item). Make a new scene deliberately different in its geometry from a style reference.

**For a character across several prompts**, write the description once and reuse it word for word.

**Offer two to four versions**, each in its own box, each labelled by what it tries, with a line on
why the choices were made. A product prompt is one filled skeleton, not versions of it.

## Slates of ads

When the ask is a set of ads rather than one image, the prompts are necessary and not sufficient:
the set has to differ in ways that matter. Same theme, meaningfully different execution. Vary two or
three of the seven axes: **concept, format, aspect ratio, persona, visual treatment, copy style,
generator**. Run the weak / strong test on every pair: if the same person would respond the same way
to two ads, one of them is doing nothing. **Slate variation never varies the product**: a product
in a slate still comes from its render and its skeleton. The method, the header and the handover
format are in `references/creative-diversification.md`.

## Video

For image to video, the image is frame one: describe only what moves, the camera, the sound and
the pacing. A camera that must not move is said plainly, then escalated ("fixed tripod, absolutely
no camera movement"). Name sounds by their source. One or two actions in a short clip. No Loop
round has graded video yet. Details in `references/models.md`.

## If Vesper is not connected

**If Vesper is not connected.** Vesper is Loop's generation tool, and it holds the model keys: it draws, grades three times, records verdicts and files feedback. Without it this still works, in a smaller way. Claude reads a picture once itself and labels that read `chat x1`, never as Vesper's grade. It writes out the exact prompt, comment line or issue text for you to paste. It never asks you for a key or an `.env` file. To connect Vesper, open Claude's settings, go to Connectors, find Vesper, click Connect and sign in with your Vesper login. If Vesper is not in the list, or the sign-in says you have no access, ask whoever runs Vesper at Loop to turn on Claude access for you.

For a product image without Vesper: write out the filled skeleton and the references in their
order, to paste into Vesper's web app, and read what comes back once, labelled as one read.

## Files

| File | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `references/craft.md` | Every lesson, with its id, the round that taught it and what holds it |
| `references/models.md` | The dated router, the per-model notes, the reference limits, video |
| `references/review.md` | How a draw is read: one read or three, judges, the set, comparing |
| `references/record.md` | What is written down for every draw and verdict, and where |
| `references/creative-diversification.md` | Slates: the axes, the test, the method, the handover |
| `references/corrections.md` | What this skill got wrong since the Loop edition, once or twice |
| `CHANGELOG.md` | What changed and why, including what the general skill said that the rounds ruled out |
| `evals/` | The skill's own cases, their rubric and their log |
